“The D-Wave annealer employs a process known as quantum annealing to solve optimization problems by finding the lowest-energy configuration of a system of superconducting qubits. Each optimization problem is first formulated as an energy landscape, defined by setting the qubit biases and coupler strengths that represent the objective function of the problem. The system begins with all qubits in a quantum superposition of possible states. During the annealing process, the Hamiltonian parameters are gradually evolved so that quantum fluctuations and entanglement guide the system through many possible configurations. As the annealing progresses, the influence of the driver Hamiltonian is reduced while that of the problem Hamiltonian is increased, allowing the system to evolve naturally toward low-energy states [Johnson, M. W. et al., Nature 473, 194–198 (2011)]. Because the connectivity of the D-Wave hardware graph (e.g., Pegasus and Zephyr topologies) does not always match the connectivity of the problem graph, minor embedding is required to map logical variables and couplings onto the available physical qubits. In this process, a single logical variable may be represented by a chain of physically connected qubits, with the chain strength tuned to preserve variable consistency during annealing. At the end of the annealing, typically within time scale of microseconds, the quantum superposition collapses, and the qubits settle into a single classical configuration corresponding to the minimum (or near-minimum) energy of the encoded problem, representing the final solution. As a commercially available quantum computing platform, D-Wave has demonstrated the ability to address certain real-world optimization problems. In this work, we use D-Wave as a representative quantum annealer to provide a hardware benchmark alongside the digital CPU and our MTJ-based probabilistic annealer.”

2. Parallel replicas: Running many independent SA trajectories in parallel increases the probability of discovering low-energy solutions within a given wall-clock time. Since each trajectory explores a different stochastic search path, selecting the best solution among a large ensemble of replicas improves both expected solution quality and time-to-solution.
Specifically, we implement the ΔE update computations within CUDA threads, and we map parallel SA replicas onto separate CUDA thread blocks. We then conduct two systematic studies: (i) to determine the optimal number of replicas, and (ii) to verify that the H100 hardware resources can support fully parallel ΔE evaluations for each test instance.
In Fig. P13a, we examine how the time-per-sweep scales with the number of replicas executed on the GPU. Here, “time-per-sweep” denotes the wall-clock time required to complete one simulated-annealing sweep (i.e., to perform n spin-flip proposals, where n is the total number of spins). We observe that the time-per-sweep begins to increase sharply beyond 1024 replicas, indicating that the available GPU parallel resources are saturated, and additional replicas are therefore forced to execute partially sequentially due to hardware scheduling limits. In Fig. P13b, we analyze the scaling of time-per-iteration, where “time-per-iteration” refers to the wall-clock time required to complete a single spin-flip proposal evaluation. We observe that, for all QAP instance sizes (number of spins ranging from 9 to 144), the time-per-iteration remains essentially constant when the number of replicas is below 1024. This indicates that the per-iteration cost does not grow with the number of spins, i.e., the effective complexity is O(1) rather than O(n). Consequently, we confirm that the H100 hardware resources are sufficient to support fully parallel ΔE evaluations for all test instances when operating with fewer than 1024 replicas.
We next investigate the algorithmic benefit obtained from running replicated SA trajectories, as summarized in Fig. P13c. Here, we use sweep-to-solution as the figure of merit, defined as the number of 95 sweeps required to reach 95% of the optimal solution. We observe that increasing the number of replicas reduces the sweep-to-solution, indicating that parallel replication improves the probability of rapidly reaching high-quality solutions. However, trade-offs should be made between the sweep-to-solution benefits and the time-per-sweep overhead caused by limited hardware resources above 1024 replicas. Fig. P13d presents the scaling of TTS95 with respect to the number of replicas. Beyond 1024 replicas, especially for larger instances (QAP scale > 7), the algorithmic benefits are not sufficient to compensate for the increased time-per-sweep overhead. Consequently, we choose 1024 replicas as the optimal configuration to obtain the most efficient SA performance.

Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. The efficient realization of a tunable random number generator is a key advantage gained by the MTJ-based implementation. In this work, STT-MTJs are employed not merely as random number generators for randomly selecting spins to update, but as tunable random number generators (p-bits in the context of probabilistic computing), where the probability of generating 0s or 1s can be flexibly adjusted by the input bias. This tunability is the essential advantage of MTJ-based random number generators in our system.
When comparing the CMOS based p-bits and MTJ based p-bits. CMOS p-bit implementations typically rely on a pseudo-random number generator (e.g., linear feedback shift registers, LFSRs) combined with a look-up tables (LUTs) to achieve non-linear tunable probability distribution, which incurs additional hardware overhead. The MTJ-based p-bit, by directly exploiting thermally activated stochastic switching, 32 provides a compact, inherently probabilistic, and scalable solution. As reported by Singh et al. [Nat. Commun. 15, 2685 (2024)], MTJ-based implementations can reduce transistor count by more than three orders of magnitude (~1200×) and energy consumption by over 70× compared with CMOS counterparts (LFSR+LUT). Consequently, the key advantage of the MTJ-based random number generator lies in its ability to provide parallel, high-speed, and tunable random sources, which are essential for probabilistic sampling processes that random numbers are extensively required.
In the Main text, our intention in using the term ‘high-quality’ randomness was to contrast the MTJ-based random number generator with the linear feedback shift register (LFSR)-based pseudo-random generator, whose output exhibits linear dependency and periodic repetition after a certain sequence length, characteristics we consider of “low-quality” randomness. ## Paper

## Abstract

Solving computationally demanding combinatorial optimization problems using conventional computing architectures is slow and energy intensive. Quantum computing could improve optimization efficiency but remains at an early stage. Probabilistic computing offers a practical near-term approach to faster optimization through stochastic techniques.

Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable spin-transfer-torque-magnetic-tunnel-junction based probabilistic processor for efficiently solving all-to-all connected quadratic assignment problems. Our system integrates 144 compact spintronics tunable random number generators with a massively parallel architecture, achieving a high Monte-Carlo sampling throughput of 14.4 million flips per second. We co-design a parallel trial annealing scheme, and the integrated system achieves a 123× speedup with 98.3% energy savings over conventional Gibbs sampling, and a 3.2× speedup with 58.3% energy savings relative to the central processing unit implementation based on a compiled language. We further benchmark performance across graphics processing unit, and D-Wave quantum annealers, showing gains in solution quality, speed, and energy efficiency.

---

## Introduction

Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) arise in diverse domains1, including scheduling2, logistics3, circuit design4 and financial management5. Accelerating the solution of COPs can broadly impact numerous businesses. However, the end of Moore’s law has led to diminishing performance improvements in general-purpose processors6, prompting a shift toward the development of quantum computer7 and domain-specific probabilistic computing hardware8-10. While quantum computing has attracted attention as a potential revolution to optimization field11, current systems have yet to demonstrate practical speedups for industrial applications and remain constrained by complexity and high cost12. This has motivated a parallel exploration of classical physics based probabilistic computing13-15. These architectures increasingly leverage emerging technologies such as spintronics16-22, optics23, memristors24, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs)25-27, and other unconventional platforms28-30.

Given that massive random number generation is a key ingredient of probabilistic computing, magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) emerge as promising spintronic candidates due to their energy and area efficiency, rooted in their inherent stochastic switching behavior and tunable switching probabilities31-34. The statistical properties of the MTJ-generated random numbers have been characterized for security-oriented applications35. Spin-transfer torque magnetic tunnel junctions (STT-MTJs), the building blocks of magnetic random-access memory (MRAM), are well suited for constructing probabilistic computing hardware36. STT-MTJs offer distinct advantages such as superior device uniformity, high complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) compatibility, compact structure, controllable switching probability, and fast switching speed in the nanosecond regime. These attributes make STT-MTJ-based tunable random number generators (RNGs) strong candidates for large-scale hardware implementations of probabilistic computing systems37-39.

In this article, we present a parallel 144 STT-MTJ based probabilistic processor for solving challenging COPs on fully connected graphs. This processor leverages STT-MTJs for both true random number generation and Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC) sampling, reducing the latency, area, and energy associated with conventional random sources35, and enabling highly efficient intrinsic probabilistic sampling in physical devices. The quadratic assignment problem (QAP) is a fundamental NP-hard problem that models facility-location assignment tasks with facility pairwise interaction costs40. Due to its factorial search space and densely coupled structure, QAP is regarded as one of the most challenging problems in combinatorial optimization, with exact solvers scaling poorly beyond small instances41. In this work, we use QAP as a representative case study to investigate the potential computational advantages of probabilistic computing. A system implementing our MTJ-based parallel-trial architecture solves a 12-city QAP 123 times faster than conventional simulated annealing executed on the same hardware, while reducing energy consumption by 98.3%. Compared to a von Neumann type central processing unit (CPU, Intel i9-14900K) based implementation using a compiled language C++, the proposed parallel architecture achieves a 3.2× speedup and 58.3% energy savings. As the system scales, both performance and energy efficiency are expected to improve proportionally, underscoring the benefits of parallelism and the suitability for large-scale optimization. Beyond classical baselines, we also benchmark the solution quality and feasibility of our system on QAP instances against the state-of-the-art D-Wave quantum annealer with both Zephyr and Pegasus topologies.

---

## Results

STT-MTJ based parallel probabilistic Ising machine

The solving strategy of probabilistic Ising machines (PIMs) involves mapping a COP to an Ising Hamiltonian, thereby connecting the optimal solution of the COP to the ground state of Ising energy landscape. In a lattice with N spins, where each spin is in states s = {s1,…,sN}, the Ising Hamiltonian (ℋ) is defined as ℋ(𝒔) = −∑N i<j Jij si sj −∑N i=1 hi si, where si and sj represent the states of the ith and jth spins, which can be either +1 or −1. Each ith spin is biased by a local field hi and interacts with the jth spin through a coupling Jij. The goal is to find the spin configuration that minimizes ℋ, i.e., the ground state. Unlike deterministic solvers, a PIM explores the solution space via stochastic spin updates, guided by a combination of energy minimization and sampling techniques such as Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling.

An STT-MTJ device consists of two ferromagnetic layers: a fixed reference layer with a stable magnetization, and a free layer whose magnetization can be switched by the STT effect49. These layers are separated by a thin magnesium oxide (MgO) insulating barrier, which enables quantum tunneling of spin polarized electrons50. When the magnetic moments of the two ferromagnetic layers are aligned parallel to each other, the device exhibits a low-resistance state, representing a spin state of +1; when they are antiparallel, it exhibits a high-resistance state, corresponding to a spin state of −1. With appropriately chosen pulse width and amplitude, STT induces stochastic switching, allowing the MTJ device to switch states with a controllable probability51.

Fig. 2a illustrates the system diagram of the STT-MTJ based PIM. The PIM comprises nine processing elements (PEs), each containing 16 STT-MTJ cells. Every 16 cells are driven by a 16-channel digital-to-analog converter (DAC) and sampled by a 16-channel analog-to-digital converter (ADC). Each STT-MTJ cell consists of one MTJ and one 3 kΩ sense resistor used for state readout. An FPGA interfaces with the STT-MTJ board to control the DACs and ADCs, and to compute the feedback signals for each MTJ cell at every annealing iteration. The feedback is based on the spin states read out by the ADCs and calculated based one energy minimization techniques, which typically involve a multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation between the coupling matrix J and the spin vector s. This architecture supports fully parallel operation of MTJ cells, providing flexibility to accommodate a wide range of algorithms that can accelerate from parallelism. A photograph of the STT-MTJ system is shown in Fig. 2b. The STT-MTJ devices are wire-bonded to red breakout boards, with each board hosting eight MTJs. Two breakout boards together with a DAC and an ADC form one PE. Custom FPGA Mezzanine Card (FMC) and FMC Plus (FMCP) to IPEX conversion boards are designed to enable high-speed data transmission between the FPGA and the MTJ board.

To achieve optimal problem-solving performance, a calibration process is performed after system setup. Based on the individual characteristics of each device, a linear transformation is applied to the input voltage amplitude of each MTJ. This transformation centralizes the probabilistic switching curves around zero and normalizes the slope at the origin to a value of 0.25. In practice, all MTJ cells are operated in parallel by fixing the DAC output pulse width to 4 µs, while sweeping the amplitude from 0.68 V to 1.34 V in steps of 4.5 mV. The choice of 4 µs perturb pulse width represents a practical trade-off between DAC/ADC speed and channel count in our proof-of-concept system. The resulting switching probability versus voltage curves for all MTJs are shown in Fig. 2c, where noticeable deviations and differences in slopes can be observed. The observed variation in MTJ switching probabilities mainly arises from fabrication-induced non-uniformities, such as variations in film thickness and etching precision. After characterizing the probabilistic switching behavior of each device, the curves are calibrated to align with a standard sigmoid function, as illustrated in Fig. 2d (see Supplementary Note 1 for details). Although the calibration cannot fully compensate for all device-to-device variations and non-idealities, it significantly improves performance, particularly by centralizing the switching curves around zero.

For large‐scale implementations (e.g., on the order of millions of MTJs), assigning distinct calibration parameters to every individual device would impose prohibitive hardware overhead. Importantly, wafer-level MRAM production has demonstrated excellent device-to-device uniformity in MTJ switching statistics. Based on this, it is reasonable to assume that only a small number of calibration parameter sets (e.g., one global set, or a few sets per process/wafer class) would be sufficient to capture the switching probability characteristics across all MTJs, without consuming significant memory resources. Furthermore, as the system scales, data transfer, particularly between memory and computing units, can substantially increase computation time. Benefiting from the CMOS compatibility, MTJ-based probabilistic computing systems can be integrated with emerging in-memory computing technologies such as MRAM52 and resistive random-access memory (RRAM)53 based platforms.

MTJ based parallel probabilistic Ising processor architecture

The digital annealer (DA) is a specialized hardware accelerator designed to solve combinatorial optimization problems by implementing a simulated annealing algorithm in a parallel-trial framework54,55. Each annealing iteration consists of two stages: a parallel-trial phase and a single-update phase. During the parallel-trial phase, the system evaluates N energy changes ΔE1, ΔE2…ΔEN in parallel, in analogy to quantum superposition, where ΔEi corresponds to the change in system energy if bipolar spin si is flipped to −si, while all other spins remain fixed. The acceptance for all proposed flips is then determined simultaneously using either the Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs sampling criteria. In the subsequent single-update phase, the system randomly selects and commits one of the accepted spin-flip candidates, ensuring at most one spin changes its state per iteration to preserve the Markov chain dynamics.

In conventional CMOS based parallel-trial architecture, pseudo random number generators (PRNGs), such as linear feedback shift registers (LFSR) and lookup tables (LUT), are typically employed in the sampling process. For example, in the case of Gibbs sampling, the probability of accepting a spin flip follows a sigmoid-like function, 1/(1+exp(βΔE)), where β is the annealing parameter. This operation generally involves using a LUT to compute the sigmoid value and a 32-bit LFSR to generate a fix-point random number uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. A comparator is then used to determine the acceptance of the proposed flip by comparing the sigmoid result and the generated random number. PRNGs are also highly demanded in the single-update phase to randomly select one spin for flipping among all accepted candidates. Given the parallel nature of architecture and the large scale of COPs, area and energy consumption scaling can become significant.

In contrast, STT-MTJs inherently exhibit a sigmoid-like stochastic switching behavior that can be exploited for both the parallel-trial phase (MCMC sampling) and the single-update phase (random selection among accepted candidates). Rather than relying on bulky LUTs and LFSRs, sampling with MTJ is reduced to a simple operation: the computed value of βΔE is converted into voltage domain and applied to an STT-MTJ, whose probabilistic switching response yields the sampling result. Random number generation, required for spin selection in the update phase, is similarly achieved by biasing the MTJ at its 50-50 switching point, where thermal noise induces stochastic transitions with approximately 50% probability. It is estimated that an MTJ-based implementation can reduce transistor count by over three orders of magnitude (~1200×) and energy consumption by more than 70× compared to conventional CMOS based 32-bit LFSR + LUT implementation56. Moreover, unlike LFSRs57, the true random numbers generated by MTJs do not exhibit periodicity, regardless of runtime duration. The inherent and tunable randomness enhances the efficiency of the system to escape local minima and explore the energy landscape more effectively58.

Fig. 3 illustrates the MTJ-based parallel-trial accelerator, implemented as a tightly coupled FPGA-MTJ system. In each annealing iteration, the FPGA computes energy changes ΔE for all spin flip trials in parallel and converts them into MTJ voltage inputs through a linear transformation. These voltages are applied to MTJ cells, with each MTJ cell functioning as a local MCMC sampler. The analog outputs of MTJ cells are digitized by on-board ADCs and fed back to the FPGA. The FPGA then compares the digitized outputs against predefined thresholds to generate acceptance flags (denoted as flag in Fig. 3) for each trial. Subsequently, all MTJ cells are perturbed at their calibrated 50-50 switching point to generate true random bits, which are utilized by the update arbiter module.

The update arbiter module adopts a multi-layer structure to select a single spin among the pool of accepted candidates. Each input node in the arbiter carries acceptance flag and spin index. At each layer, a selector evaluates the two input nodes: if both have flags set to 1, one spin index is randomly forwarded based on MTJ-generated random bits; if only one flag is 1, that spin index is passed through; and if both flags are 0, a null index with flag 0 propagates. This arbitration process continues across layers until a single spin index is selected for update, ensuring that at most one spin is flipped per annealing iteration.

Evaluation on quadratic assignment problems

We evaluate the performance of our STT-MTJ based parallel-trial accelerator using problem instances from the tinyQAP dataset59. This dataset includes QAP instances with sizes ranging from 3 to 12 facilities and locations (see Supplementary Note 2 for additional tests on large instances). The mapping from the QAP to the Ising model follows the quadratic scaling rule: each QAP instance with n facilities and locations is transformed into an Ising model comprising n2 spins. As a result, the corresponding Ising graphs span from fully connected 9 to 144 spins.

In the conventional simulated annealing (SA) scheme, only one spin-flip proposal is evaluated and updated in an annealing iteration. Therefore, using a single MTJ to sequentially update all spins is equivalent to using n2 MTJs to update all spins, without any loss in speed or energy consumption. Based on this, we use a single STT-MTJ for spin update in our system for SA. However, in the parallel-trial annealing (PA) scheme, where all spin-flip proposals must be evaluated simultaneously. The number of MTJ devices should match the number of spins in the Ising model to fully exploit parallelism. Leveraging the massive parallel architecture of our STT-MTJ based system, we utilize 2n2−1 MTJs in parallel for spin update in the PA scheme, where n2 MTJs are used for MCMC sampling, and n2−1 MTJs function as random number generators for the arbiter module during the single-update phase.

We benchmark our MTJ-based probabilistic Ising processor against digital platforms, including a high-performance Intel i9-14900K CPU and an NVIDIA H100 GPU, on QAP instances. On the CPU, we implement simulated annealing in both an interpreted environment (MATLAB) and a compiled environment (C++) to provide a fair comparison across different software execution paradigms. On the GPU, we implemented replicated simulated annealing (replicated SA) in C++ environment. Specifically, we implement the ΔE update computations within CUDA threads and assign 1024 independent SA replicas to separate CUDA thread blocks. Further GPU implementation details are provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Fig. 4a presents the median time to reach 95% of the optimal solution (TTS95) as a function of problem scale, measured by the number of spins in the Ising model. All computing platforms are evaluated under an identical annealing schedule to ensure a controlled comparison. Relative to MTJ-SA, the MTJ-PA scheme exhibits a substantial acceleration, achieving speedup factors of up to 123×. When benchmarked against CPU-based SA, MTJ-PA provides improvements of up to 6.6× over the interpreted-language MATLAB implementation and 3.2× over the compiled-language C++ implementation. In comparison with GPU-based replicated SA, MTJ-PA attains up to 8.9× acceleration. It should be noted that, in our current implementation, the GPU and CPU exhibit comparable performance. This behavior arises because the problem sizes used in our present evaluation are not sufficiently large for the massive parallelism of GPU to yield a significant advantage. For relatively small instances, the overhead associated with GPU kernel launches and data movement offsets the benefits of parallel execution, leading to performance similar to that of the CPU.

When comparing MTJ-SA with CPU-SA, we observe that the MTJ-based SA operates more slowly than its CPU counterpart, primarily due to peripheral circuit limitations in our proof-of-concept system, most notably the constrained DAC/ADC throughput (see Supplementary Note 4 for a detailed system-latency analysis). Despite this limitation, the MTJ-based PA still substantially accelerates the annealing process by leveraging both the algorithmic advantage of a higher spin-flip acceptance rate and the parallel architecture enabled by tunable MTJ-based random number generators. To further enhance the performance of MTJ-based probabilistic computing systems, future implementations can leverage tighter MTJ-CMOS integration through back-end-of-line (BEOL) technologies to achieve more compact architecture. By co-integrating MTJs with on-chip high-speed DACs, sense amplifiers, and local control logic, the overall system latency can be significantly reduced. With MTJs operating at their intrinsic switching limit, on the order of 250 million flips per second per device38,60, the achievable acceleration could approach four orders of magnitude compared to CPU-based implementations. Such a speedup is also expected to improve solution quality within the given runtime budget. It is also worth noting that we use a simple linearly increasing inverse temperature schedule, without any fine-tuning or specialized optimization. Incorporating more advanced algorithmic techniques61 into our architecture could further improve performance.

Fig. 4b presents the median energy-to-solution (ETS) scaling, including energy consumption from FPGA, DACs, ADCs and MTJs as a function of QAP problem size (represented by the number of spins). The energy-to-solution is estimated by multiplying the system power (see Method for details) by the corresponding time-to-solution. Although MTJ-PA consumes more instantaneous power than MTJ-SA due to its parallel architecture (see Supplementary Note 5 for details), it still achieves lower overall energy consumption because of the significant reduction in TTS. The energy saving factor is defined as 1−(ETS_MTJ-PA /ETS_other scheme), where ETS_MTJ-PA and ETS_other scheme represent the energy-to-solution of MTJ-PA and other schemes. The energy-saving factor between MTJ-PA and MTJ-SA increases with the level of parallelism, reaching 98.3% in our system. When compared to CPU-SA, the MTJ-PA achieves 87.1% energy savings over the interpreted-language MATLAB implementation and 58.3% over the compiled-language C++ implementation, demonstrating the significant efficiency advantage of MTJ-based stochastic computing.

Benchmark digital, probabilistic and quantum computing

To assess the performance of conventional digital computing, classical physics-based probabilistic computing, and quantum computing in solving complex optimization problems, we benchmarked representative platforms on a series of fully connected QAPs with sizes ranging from 3 to 12. For digital computing, we implement a simulated annealing algorithm on a CPU with 5000 sweeps, where each sweep consists of attempted updates for every spins. For probabilistic computing, we employ a parallel-trial annealing scheme on our STT-MTJ-based probabilistic Ising machine, running for 5000 iterations, with each iteration updating at most one spin. For quantum computing, we benchmark with the state-of-the-art D-Wave quantum annealer.

The D-Wave annealer employs a process known as quantum annealing to solve optimization problems by finding the lowest-energy configuration of a system of superconducting qubits. Each optimization problem is first formulated as an energy landscape, defined by setting the qubit biases and coupler strengths that represent the objective function of the problem. The system begins with all qubits in a quantum superposition of possible states. During the annealing process, the Hamiltonian parameters are gradually evolved so that quantum fluctuations and entanglement guide the system through many possible configurations. As the anneal progresses, the influence of the driver Hamiltonian is reduced while that of the problem Hamiltonian is increased, allowing the system to evolve naturally toward low-energy states62. Because the connectivity of the D-Wave hardware graph (e.g., Pegasus and Zephyr topologies) does not always match the connectivity of the problem graph, minor embedding is required to map logical variables and couplings onto the available physical qubits. In this process, a single logical variable may be represented by a chain of physically connected qubits, with the chain strength tuned to preserve variable consistency during annealing. At the end of the anneal, typically within time scale of microseconds, the quantum superposition collapses, and the qubits settle into a single classical configuration corresponding to the minimum (or near-minimum) energy of the encoded problem, representing the final solution. As a commercially available quantum computing platform, D-Wave has demonstrated the ability to address certain real-world optimization problems. Thus, in this work, we use D-Wave as a representative quantum annealer to provide a hardware benchmark alongside the digital CPU and our MTJ-based probabilistic annealer. CPU-SA performs slightly worse than MTJ-PA but remains comparably close to the optimum. In the quantum computing regime, both D-Wave Zephyr and D-Wave Pegasus can find feasible solutions for QAP instances with fewer than four facilities and locations. ## Methods

Thin film growth and device fabrication. Thin film stacks with the structure: substrate/[W (3)/Ru (10)]₂/W (3)/Pt (3)/Co (0.25)/Pt (0.2)/[Co (0.25)/Pt (0.5)]5/Co (0.6)/Ru (0.85)/Co (0.6)/Pt (0.2)/Co (0.3)/Pt (0.2)/Co (0.5)/W (0.3)/CoFeB (0.9)/MgO (0.85)/CoFeB (1.2)/W (0.4)/CoFeB (0.8)/MgO (0.7)/Ta (3)/Ru (7)/Ta (5) (thicknesses in nanometers) were deposited on Si substrates with a 300 nm thermal oxide layer. The deposition was carried out at room temperature using direct current (DC) magnetron sputtering for metallic layers and radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering for MgO, under a base pressure below 2 × 10⁻8 Torr. To fabricate the MTJ devices, 10 µm-wide bottom electrode structures were first patterned via photolithography and Ar ion milling. MTJ pillars with ~90nm diameter were then defined using electron beam lithography. Following ion milling, an Si3N4 encapsulation layer was deposited in situ using RF magnetron sputtering, without breaking vacuum. Finally, 10 µm-wide top electrode structures were patterned using photolithography, and the top electrode layers, Ta (5 nm)/Cu (40 nm), were deposited using DC magnetron sputtering.

MTJ carrier printed circuit board (PCB) design. Sixteen 16-channel DACs (AD5767) are used to generate analog input to each MTJ, and sixteen 16-channel ADCs (MAX11131) are used to sample the output of each MTJ cell and send to the FPGA (AMD Virtex UltraScale+ FPGA VCU118 Evaluation Kit) for feedback signal calculation. The polarity of Vin dictates the current direction such that the reset and perturb processes can be realized. Both DACs and ADCs interface with the FPGA through serial peripheral interface (SPI) protocol via IPEX hardware connection. The RTL logic in FPGA is programmed and implemented in Vivado 2023.2 platform using Verilog. In our setup, the main clock frequency in the FPGA is set to 100 MHz. For QAP instances with scale > 8, we use two MTJ carrier PCBs connected to the FPGA via IPEX and controlled in parallel by the VCU118. One PCB serves solely as a random number generator bank, with its MTJs biased at the 50-50 switching probability point to supply random numbers to the update-arbiter module.

Matrix-vector multiplication in FPGA. In the parallel-trial phase, each trial assumes a single spin flip while all other spins remain fixed. Under this assumption, the energy change term ΔEi associated with spin si flip to −si is given by: ΔEi = −2siLi, where Li(𝒔) = hi +∑N j=1 Jij sj. All the initial Li values are precalculated and stored in registers, as illustrated in Fig. 3 blue block. When a spin state is updated, each Li is incrementally updated by adding its corresponding change Li. For example, when sj is flipped to −sj, the resulting increment Li = Jij (−2sj).

TTS estimation. In the FPGA design, an integrated logic analyzer (ILA) is implemented to probe the current state of the finite state machine (FSM) that controls the annealing process. The duration of a single annealing iteration can be measured using the ILA, and multiplying this duration by the number of iterations required to reach a solution yields the total TTS.

System power estimation. For the MTJ-based system, the total power consumption was estimated as the sum of the FPGA, ADC/DAC, and MTJ contributions. The FPGA power was obtained from the Vivado Power Report generated after design implementation. The ADC and DAC power values were calculated from their respective supply voltage and current specifications. The MTJ power was estimated by summing the consumption during the reset and perturb phases. For the CPU-based implementation, the power consumption is estimated by multiplying the CPU utilization rate of the program (MATLAB or C++ executable) during runtime by the nominal power rating of the processor. For the GPU-based implementation, we estimate a light-load power baseline of 90 W.

Data availability. The data that support the findings of this study are available within the article and the Supplementary Information.

In a single-threaded CPU implementation, the parallel-trial annealing algorithm can only be emulated sequentially, as the CPU executes one instruction at a time. As a result, for a problem with n spins, the CPU based PA requires O(n) time per iteration to evaluate all spin flip proposals, which is effectively equivalent to one simulated annealing (SA) sweep. In contrast, on parallel hardware, all spins can be evaluated simultaneously, resulting in a time complexity of O(1) per iteration.
As shown in Fig. P7, we compare the time-to-solution of CPU-based SA, CPU-based PA, and MTJ-based SA and PA. For small problem sizes (e.g., scale below 7), the CPU-SA performs slightly better compared to CPU-PA because the CPU-PA implementation includes an additional arbiter process in each iteration to stochastically select among update candidates, which slightly increases the time consumption per iteration. However, starting from problem scale 8, CPU-PA begins to show modest improvement due to its ability to increase spin flip proposal acceptance probability. MTJ-based PA continues to outperform CPU-PA as the problem scales up, benefiting from the hardware-level parallelism inherent to the architecture, where all spin updates are evaluated concurrently.

Each optimization problem is first formulated as an energy landscape, defined by setting the qubit biases and coupler strengths that represent the objective function of the problem. The system begins with all qubits in a quantum superposition of possible states. In this process, a single logical variable may be represented by a chain of physically connected qubits, with the chain strength tuned to preserve variable consistency during annealing. At the end of the annealing, typically within time scale of microseconds, the quantum superposition collapses, and the qubits settle into a single classical configuration corresponding to the minimum (or near-minimum) energy of the encoded problem, representing the final solution. As a commercially available quantum computing platform, D-Wave has demonstrated the ability to address certain real-world optimization problems. 2. Parallel replicas: Running many independent SA trajectories in parallel increases the probability of discovering low-energy solutions within a given wall-clock time. Since each trajectory explores a different stochastic search path, selecting the best solution among a large ensemble of replicas improves both expected solution quality and time-to-solution.
Specifically, we implement the ΔE update computations within CUDA threads, and we map parallel SA replicas onto separate CUDA thread blocks. We then conduct two systematic studies: (i) to determine the optimal number of replicas, and (ii) to verify that the H100 hardware resources can support fully parallel ΔE evaluations for each test instance.
In Fig. P13a, we examine how the time-per-sweep scales with the number of replicas executed on the GPU. Here, “time-per-sweep” denotes the wall-clock time required to complete one simulated-annealing sweep (i.e., to perform n spin-flip proposals, where n is the total number of spins). We observe that the time-per-sweep begins to increase sharply beyond 1024 replicas, indicating that the available GPU parallel resources are saturated, and additional replicas are therefore forced to execute partially sequentially due to hardware scheduling limits. In Fig. P13b, we analyze the scaling of time-per-iteration, where “time-per-iteration” refers to the wall-clock time required to complete a single spin-flip proposal evaluation. We observe that, for all QAP instance sizes (number of spins ranging from 9 to 144), the time-per-iteration remains essentially constant when the number of replicas is below 1024. This indicates that the per-iteration cost does not grow with the number of spins, i.e., the effective complexity is O(1) rather than O(n). Consequently, we confirm that the H100 hardware resources are sufficient to support fully parallel ΔE evaluations for all test instances when operating with fewer than 1024 replicas.
We next investigate the algorithmic benefit obtained from running replicated SA trajectories, as summarized in Fig. P13c. Here, we use sweep-to-solution as the figure of merit, defined as the number of 95 sweeps required to reach 95% of the optimal solution. We observe that increasing the number of replicas reduces the sweep-to-solution, indicating that parallel replication improves the probability of rapidly reaching high-quality solutions. However, trade-offs should be made between the sweep-to-solution benefits and the time-per-sweep overhead caused by limited hardware resources above 1024 replicas. Fig. P13d presents the scaling of TTS95 with respect to the number of replicas. Beyond 1024 replicas, especially for larger instances (QAP scale > 7), the algorithmic benefits are not sufficient to compensate for the increased time-per-sweep overhead. Consequently, we choose 1024 replicas as the optimal configuration to obtain the most efficient SA performance.

This means that, in order for the GPU-replicated SA to ultimately outperform the CPU in time-to-solution, it would need to reach the target solution in only ~1/4 to 1/5 as many sweeps. Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. The efficient realization of a tunable random number generator is a key advantage gained by the MTJ-based implementation. In this work, STT-MTJs are employed not merely as random number generators for randomly selecting spins to update, but as tunable random number generators (p-bits in the context of probabilistic computing), where the probability of generating 0s or 1s can be flexibly adjusted by the input bias. This tunability is the essential advantage of MTJ-based random number generators in our system.
When comparing the CMOS based p-bits and MTJ based p-bits. CMOS p-bit implementations typically rely on a pseudo-random number generator (e.g., linear feedback shift registers, LFSRs) combined with a look-up tables (LUTs) to achieve non-linear tunable probability distribution, which incurs additional hardware overhead. The MTJ-based p-bit, by directly exploiting thermally activated stochastic switching, 32 provides a compact, inherently probabilistic, and scalable solution. As reported by Singh et al. [Nat. Commun. 15, 2685 (2024)], MTJ-based implementations can reduce transistor count by more than three orders of magnitude (~1200×) and energy consumption by over 70× compared with CMOS counterparts (LFSR+LUT). Consequently, the key advantage of the MTJ-based random number generator lies in its ability to provide parallel, high-speed, and tunable random sources, which are essential for probabilistic sampling processes that random numbers are extensively required.
In the Main text, our intention in using the term ‘high-quality’ randomness was to contrast the MTJ-based random number generator with the linear feedback shift register (LFSR)-based pseudo-random generator, whose output exhibits linear dependency and periodic repetition after a certain sequence length, characteristics we consider of “low-quality” randomness. In contrast, the MTJ-based random number generator produces stochastic outputs that do not exhibit linear dependency or periodicity, regardless of runtime, owing to its thermally activated switching nature. However, we agree with the reviewer that the term ‘high-quality’ can be vague in this context, as from a statistical perspective, similar to other true random number generator implementations, the raw output of our MTJ-based source does not fully satisfy stringent statistical tests such as the NIST 800-22 suite without post-processing. As demonstrated in our prior work ([Ng et al., Phys. Rev. Appl. 19, 034077 (2023)], the NIST 800-22 results are summarized in Table P4 under “Raw data”), the unprocessed sequence does not pass all the tests. Furthermore, analysis using the NIST 800-90B indicates a min-entropy of 0.778584 bits per output bit, confirming that the entropy is below the ideal value of 1.
For security-oriented applications, such entropy reduction necessitates post-processing to enhance statistical uniformity. Accordingly, we applied Toeplitz hashing to the raw output, and the processed (Extracted) data successfully passed the NIST SP 800-22 tests, as shown in Table P6. Thus, in this case, the MTJ should be regarded as an entropy source for a true random number generator, which requires an additional post-processing unit to form a complete TRNG system.
However, for probabilistic computing tasks such as MCMC sampling, the algorithmic performance is not highly sensitive to exact statistical distributions. Instead, scalability, tunability, and speed are the more dominant factors. Therefore, in this study, post-processing for statistical enhancement was not applied, as the focus was on the tunable probabilistic behavior.
In the Main text, we have therefore replaced the term “high-quality randomness” with “inherent and tunable randomness.” The revised sentence now reads: “The inherent and tunable randomness enhances the efficiency of the system to escape local minima and explore the energy landscape more effectively.”.
